description:
What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

description:
What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, web_object is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas too.

It is also not fully documented either, but I use it since several
years to augment my own Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it
works fairly well; it also explains why this project has to stay
flexible, e. g. if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015, and
admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider them still 
to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love simplicity. Compare
a hello-world example in a .cgi script with one in rails.

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
This project will attempt to 'convert' yaml files into bash-rc files,
that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48282 registered
aliases.

description:
What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

description:
This library is called opn. It will simply output the
    name of the class. Optionally, you can assign another
    namespace to report with. For an explanation, just
    look at the few examples under the test/ directory.

    Why did I write it?

    I wrote many different ruby classes, and sometimes they will
    report information to me, but I don't know which file wrote
    this. So I wanted to simply have output prefaced with the
    name of the class in question, optionally to be colourized
    as well, since that helps me on the commandline.

    The name "opn" stands for "output program name".

    Version 1.0.2 now has a proper module, called Opn,
    and Opn has only one method called opn().

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, web_object is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas too.

It is also not fully documented either, but I use it since several
years to augment my own Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it
works fairly well; it also explains why this project has to stay
flexible, e. g. if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015, and
admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider them still 
to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love simplicity. Compare
a hello-world example in a .cgi script with one in rails.

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, web_object is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas too.

It is also not fully documented either, but I use it since several
years to augment my own Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it
works fairly well; it also explains why this project has to stay
flexible, e. g. if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015, and
admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider them still 
to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love simplicity. Compare
a hello-world example in a .cgi script with one in rails.

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

Essentially, this project is a collection of different ruby scripts/classes

but also allow installation from binary, from a remote or from a local
location (e. g. a file in a directory on the local harddisc/SSD).

There are presently 3731 registered
programs available as part of the RBT project.

gem ( or simply visit the following link: https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/rbt/ )

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, web_object is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas too.

It is also not fully documented either, but I use it since several
years to augment my own Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it
works fairly well; it also explains why this project has to stay
flexible, e. g. if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015, and
admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider them still 
to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love simplicity. Compare
a hello-world example in a .cgi script with one in rails.

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Oedipus Lex is a lexer generator in the same family as Rexical and
Rex. Oedipus Lex is my independent lexer fork of Rexical. Rexical was
in turn a fork of Rex. We've been unable to contact the author of rex
in order to take it over, fix it up, extend it, and relicense it to
MIT. So, Oedipus was written clean-room in order to bypass licensing
constraints (and because bootstrapping is fun).

Oedipus brings a lot of extras to the table and at this point is only
historically related to rexical. The syntax has changed enough that
any rexical lexer will have to be tweaked to work inside of oedipus.
At the very least, you need to add slashes to all your regexps.

Oedipus, like rexical, is based primarily on generating code much like
you would a hand-written lexer. It is _not_ a table or hash driven
lexer. It uses StrScanner within a multi-level case statement. As such,
Oedipus matches on the _first_ match, not the longest (like lex and
its ilk).

This documentation is not meant to bypass any prerequisite knowledge
on lexing or parsing. If you'd like to study the subject in further
detail, please try [TIN321] or the [LLVM Tutorial] or some other good
resource for CS learning. Books... books are good. I like books.
summary: Oedipus Lex is a lexer generator in the same family as Rexical and Rex

description:
This project will attempt to 'convert' yaml files into bash-rc files,
that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48308 registered
aliases.

Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas too.

It is also not fully documented either, but I use it since several
years to augment my own Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it
works fairly well; it also explains why this project has to stay
flexible, e. g. if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015, and
admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider them still 
to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love simplicity. Compare
a hello-world example in a .cgi script with one in rails.

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas too.

It is also not fully documented either, but I use it since several
years to augment my own Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it
works fairly well; it also explains why this project has to stay
flexible, e. g. if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015, and
admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider them still 
to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love simplicity. Compare
a hello-world example in a .cgi script with one in rails.

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

successor to the older gtk_module project.

It extends the Gtk/Gdk part of both ruby-gtk2 / ruby-gtk3,

mapping to the C source code. Some custom widgets are
also created, to make working with the ruby-gtk
bindings easier.

This project is very beta-ish, though. Do not yet use it
in production unless you are willing for things to break
all over everywhere. :)

For more information, please have a look at the documentation
for this gem, at:

description:
What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

all over everywhere. :)

for this gem, at:

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

This library is called html_tags. Its basic core idea is to collect all valid html tags into a single project, and then make this data available to other projects. Other ideas are to autogenerate closing tags (helper methods), and of course to generate string representations of these html tags. This can then be used by other web-projects. A simple usage example follows: require 'html_tags' HtmlTags.p 'hello world!' # => "

hello world!

" Since Version 0.0.10 (April 2014) we can also now query whether a string contains only valid HTML tags or whether it does not.

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

This project will attempt to 'convert' yaml files into bash-rc files,
that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48364 registered
aliases.

description:
This library is called opn. It will simply output the
    name of the class. Optionally, you can assign another
    namespace to report with. For an explanation, just
    look at the few examples under the test/ directory.

    Why did I write it?

    I wrote many different ruby classes, and sometimes they will
    report information to me, but I don't know which file wrote
    this. So I wanted to simply have output prefaced with the
    name of the class in question, optionally to be colourized
    as well, since that helps me on the commandline.

    The name "opn" stands for "output program name".

    Version 1.0.2 now has a proper module, called Opn,
    and Opn has only one method called opn().

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

computer host system, in particular on Linux systems, if ruby is available
on that computer. Commonly used programs will be queried for their current
version number (and whether they exist) on the target computer. If these
programs do happen to exist then the corresponding version will be
displayed, on the commandline.

a shell script to display the version of many commonly used programs.
As I prefer ruby over shell scripts, I wrote this somewhat equivalent
project.

For more information and documentation about this project, consider
looking at the homepage of this gem, at

  https://rubygems.org/gems/environment_information

and look at the documentation on the bottom right side,
called "Documentation".

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:

description:
This class can be used to save a file in a convenient way,
by giving you a very simple save-file functionality.

I liked the name 'save_file()' a lot, and I found that I
was  needing such a functionality in many of my projects,
so I made a tiny gem that would do exactly this. Note
that the recommended methods are write_what_into() and
append_what_into() - at the least for me, this is easy
to remember.

Of course you can use File.open() or File.new() already
as-is in block variant, so there is no need to use a 
gem like this one here - but I did not want to have to
deal with file permissions or missing files or similar
all on my own, via the File API that I do not as easily
remember. So I just wrote an API that is simple enough
for my use cases. 

Usage examples:

    require 'save_file'
    save_what_into('test', '/tmp/test.txt')

You can also use:

    SaveFile.write_what_into(what, into)
    SaveFile.append_what_into(what, into)

The main module can be included into a class,
which then will have these methods available.

This project has no external dependencies, deliberately 
so. It has to remain stand-alone.

Version 1.0.3 made it more clear when to use save_file()
and when to use append_into_file().

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

description:
The gem environment_information is able to provide information about the
computer host system, in particular on Linux systems, if ruby is available
on that computer. Commonly used programs will be queried for their current
version number (and whether they exist) on the target computer. If these
programs do happen to exist then the corresponding version will be
displayed, on the commandline.

This is somewhat similar to the "Linux from Scratch" project, which uses
a shell script to display the version of many commonly used programs.
As I prefer ruby over shell scripts, I wrote this somewhat equivalent
project.

For more information and documentation about this project, consider
looking at the homepage of this gem, at

  https://rubygems.org/gems/environment_information

and look at the documentation on the bottom right side,
called "Documentation".

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
This project will attempt to 'convert' yaml files into bash-rc files,
that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48414 registered
aliases.

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

description:
The gem environment_information is able to provide information about the
computer host system, in particular on Linux systems, if ruby is available
on that computer. Commonly used programs will be queried for their current
version number (and whether they exist) on the target computer. If these
programs do happen to exist then the corresponding version will be
displayed, on the commandline.

This is somewhat similar to the "Linux from Scratch" project, which uses
a shell script to display the version of many commonly used programs.
As I prefer ruby over shell scripts, I wrote this somewhat equivalent
project.

For more information and documentation about this project, consider
looking at the homepage of this gem, at

  https://rubygems.org/gems/environment_information

and look at the documentation on the bottom right side,
called "Documentation".

that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48438 registered
aliases.

description:
This project will attempt to 'convert' yaml files into bash-rc files,
that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48447 registered
aliases.

description:
This project will attempt to 'convert' yaml files into bash-rc files,
that is, resource files that can be loaded up in bash or in other 
shells, such as zsh or fish.

The project comes with aliases pre-defined to navigate the local
filesystem, defaulting to a Linux filesystem. There are also aliases
for various programs - program shortcuts such as 'gi' being an alias
for 'gimp', and many other aliases.

Note that the default bundled distribution refers to my own use cases,
which may be quite useless to other people. That is why this project
allows you to load your own custom dataset, as .yml file, and use
it instead. Please have a look at the documentation for more 
information as to how this is done.

Currently this gem contains a total of
48453 registered
aliases.

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
Cyberweb is a tool-set project for the www, including an incomplete
web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

For more information about the web_object project, while keeping
i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
documentation link towards the right hand side on the homepage
of this gem, at:

    https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/cyberweb/

description:
What is this project all about?

This project is primarily for my custom ruby-related stuff.

It may not be hugely important for other ruby users, but in the
event that someone may want to re-use / modify any of the code,
this project is available on rubygems.org as well.

When I am at a new computer, and ruby is available on that machine
in any way (or if I can compile a version of ruby on that machine),
then the roebe gem is the gem that I will install first, usually,
together with the gem called colours.

The roebe gem acts, sort of, as my "basic working tools", code that
I can use daily, written in ruby. As such, the project has lots of
different goals, and is a bit chaotic; it is a toolset project
that helps me solve common (and not so common) problems.

Since as of March 2018, this project also includes a slightly
modified version of setup.rb - I needed this oldschool ruby file
available in the event that an installation via gems would fail.

For more documentation about this project, please have a look at the
official homepage of this gem at rubygems.org, at its documentation/
link on the bottom right hand side (or just use this link directly:
https://www.rubydoc.info/gems/roebe/ )

web "framework". The project attempts to explore different ideas,
so it has a somewhat medium-to-large size as-is.

As a project, cyberweb is quite far away from being complete or
reasonably finished - consider it more as a proof-of-concept
project than something that should be used in production. In
fact, I use the project to explore new, web-related ideas 
all of the time.

The cyberweb project in its present state is not fully documented
either, which is unfortunate - I intend to improve on the documentation
over time.

The project is used since many years years to augment my own 
Ruby-CGI scripts. For these basic needs it works fairly well; 
it also explains why this project has to stay flexible, e. g. 
if I am to use sinatra rather than .cgi. In fact, since as of
May 2021, I am using the cyberweb toolkit as a way to improve
on sinatra-related functionality as well.

While .cgi scripts are not that common to see past the year 2015,
and admittedly not as flexible as sinatra or rails, I consider 
them still  to be extremely SIMPLE to use and I really love
simplicity. Compare a hello-world example in a .cgi script
with one in rails; in my opinion, the cgi example is much,
much simpler. I don't refer to the default cgi in ruby, 
though, which is admittedly horrible - otherwise I would not
have had a need to create this project. :)

If you need a framework that is more sophisticated, I can recommend
sinatra and padrino.

i mind that it is incomplete as-it-is, have a look at the
